q: Past practical exam (2011–2012 sets): answer the questions on the slide.
a:
Contrast-enhanced CT – chronic pancreatitis

Two changes: pancreatic calcifications and a dilated (moniliform) Wirsung duct; ± atrophy, pseudocysts. Steatorrhoea = exocrine insufficiency.
src: Practical exam sets 2011–2012 (answers written for the site)

q: Past practical exam (2011–2012 sets): answer the questions on the slide.
a:
Liver ultrasound – multiple liver metastases

Multiple hypoechoic nodules of varying size scattered in both lobes.
src: Practical exam sets 2011–2012 (answers written for the site)

q: Past practical exam (2011–2012 sets): answer the questions on the slide.
a:
Multiphase contrast CT – hepatic haemangioma

Peripheral, nodular (globular) enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal fill-in on portal and delayed phases.
src: Practical exam sets 2011–2012 (answers written for the site)

q: Past practical exam (2011–2012 sets): answer the questions on the slide.
a:
Contrast-enhanced CT – pancreatic tumour (adenocarcinoma)

Hypodense, poorly enhancing pancreatic mass (arrow) deforming the contour; check duct dilatation, vascular invasion, liver metastases.
src: Practical exam sets 2011–2012 (answers written for the site)

q: Past practical exam (2011–2012 sets): answer the questions on the slide.
a:
MRCP – hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin) with intrahepatic biliary dilatation

Heavily T2-weighted fluid image: dilated intrahepatic ducts converging on a hilar stricture.
src: Practical exam sets 2011–2012 (answers written for the site)

q: Past practical exam (2011–2012 sets): answer the questions on the slide.
a:
Liver ultrasound – hydatid cyst (multivesicular, with daughter cysts)

Cystic lesion containing multiple daughter cysts ("honeycomb/rosette").
src: Practical exam sets 2011–2012 (answers written for the site)

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Chronic pancreatitis

Pancreatic CALCIFICATIONS, irregular moniliform dilatation of the Wirsung duct, atrophy, pseudocysts; focal form mimics carcinoma.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Pancreatic head tumour

Hypodense/hypoechoic poorly enhancing mass in the head, double-duct sign, upstream atrophy; assess SMA/SMV encasement.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Inflammatory bowel disease (US)

Thickened bowel wall (> 3–4 mm), loss of layering, hyperaemia on Doppler, non-compressible loop, inflamed surrounding fat.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Acute appendicitis

US: non-compressible blind-ending tube > 6 mm, target appearance, hyperechoic inflamed fat, ± appendicolith (shadow) and periappendiceal fluid. CT if doubtful.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Peritonitis with ascites

Free fluid with bowel loops "floating" in it, thickened enhancing peritoneum, inflamed fat.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Normal liver vs steatosis

Steatosis: liver brighter than renal cortex (hyperechoic), posterior attenuation, poor visibility of vessels/diaphragm; CT liver < spleen density.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Hepatocellular carcinoma

Cirrhotic liver; arterial-phase hyperenhancement + portal/delayed WASH-OUT + capsule (LI-RADS 5); portal vein tumour thrombus.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Peritonitis with ascites

Free fluid with bowel loops "floating" in it, thickened enhancing peritoneum, inflamed fat.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver cirrhosis

Nodular contour, coarse echotexture, hypertrophy of caudate/left lobe, atrophy of right lobe; portal hypertension (splenomegaly, ascites, collaterals).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Cystic pancreatic tumour

Cystic pancreatic mass: serous (microcystic, central scar), mucinous (macrocystic, septa, wall calcification), IPMN (duct communication).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Intestinal occlusion with peritonitis

Distended fluid-filled loops (round structures on US/CT), absent peristalsis, free fluid.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Acute (oedematous) pancreatitis

Diffusely enlarged, hypoechoic/hypodense pancreas with blurred contours and peripancreatic fluid; CECT (72 h) grades severity (necrosis = non-enhancing parenchyma).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver metastases – bull's eye

Hypoechoic halo around an iso/hyperechoic centre ("target/bull's eye") – typical of metastases.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Focal nodular hyperplasia

Young woman; homogeneous lesion with intense arterial enhancement, iso in portal phase, CENTRAL SCAR and "spoke-wheel" vessels on Doppler.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver haemangioma

Most common benign liver tumour: well-defined hyperechoic lesion on US; CT/MRI peripheral nodular (globular) enhancement with centripetal fill-in; T2 "light bulb".

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver metastasis

Usually multiple nodules of varying size; hypoattenuating in the portal phase (most); hypervascular ones (NET, RCC, melanoma) enhance arterially. Often displace vessels.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Hydatid cyst

Echinococcus: cyst with double wall, floating membranes ("water lily"), daughter cysts ("honeycomb"), wall calcification (Gharbi I–V).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver abscess

Hypoechoic complex collection with thick irregular wall, debris, ± AIR bubbles (bright echoes with reverberation); CT rim enhancement.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric cancer (infiltrative)

Linitis plastica (scirrhous): diffusely thickened, rigid, non-distensible stomach ("leather bottle").

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Calcified hydatid cyst

Thick peripheral (eggshell) or complete calcification of a liver cyst = inactive/healed (Gharbi type V).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Biliary (simple) cyst

Anechoic, round, thin imperceptible wall, posterior acoustic enhancement; CT water density, no enhancement; MRI T2 bright.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Cystic liver metastasis

Cystic lesion with thick irregular hyperechoic wall, internal echoes, mural nodules – not a simple cyst (ovarian, colorectal mucinous, GIST).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Carcinomatous ascites

Free fluid with peritoneal nodules/omental "cake", loops tethered; complex fluid with septa suggests malignancy.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gallstone

Hyperechoic focus with posterior ACOUSTIC SHADOW that moves with position change; US is the method of choice.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Pancreatic tumour (body)

Hypodense mass of the pancreatic body, dilated upstream duct, celiac/SMA involvement.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gallbladder polyp

Fixed echogenic wall projection WITHOUT acoustic shadow (unlike a stone, which is mobile and shadows).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Double-duct sign

Simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct → pancreatic head (or ampullary) tumour until proven otherwise.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver cirrhosis

Nodular contour, coarse echotexture, hypertrophy of caudate/left lobe, atrophy of right lobe; portal hypertension (splenomegaly, ascites, collaterals).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Extrahepatic cholestasis

Dilated intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts (CBD > 7 mm) – look for the level and cause (stone, pancreatic head tumour, cholangiocarcinoma).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Acute pancreatitis

Enlarged pancreas, peripancreatic fat stranding and fluid collections; complications: necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess, vascular thrombosis/pseudoaneurysm.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Pancreatic tumour

Focal hypodense mass deforming the contour with duct dilatation; adenocarcinoma is hypovascular.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Splenomegaly

Spleen longer than 12–13 cm, rounded poles, extends below the costal margin (portal hypertension, haematological disease, infection).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gallbladder cholesterolosis / polyps

Non-shadowing, non-mobile echogenic wall foci; cholesterol polyps have no Doppler flow; > 10 mm polyps → cholecystectomy.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Colonic diverticulosis

Multiple round addition images (barium-filled outpouchings) mainly in the sigmoid; CT for diverticulitis.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Wall rigidity (barium)

A wall segment that does not change shape with peristalsis/compression – sign of infiltrative malignancy.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gallstone

Hyperechoic focus with posterior ACOUSTIC SHADOW that moves with position change; US is the method of choice.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Incisura (notch) – barium semiology

Indentation of the contour: on the greater curvature opposite a lesser-curvature ulcer (spasm, "pointing finger").

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Diverticulum – addition image

ADDITION image: barium-filled outpouching projecting beyond the normal contour, with a neck.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Fistula (barium)

Abnormal track of contrast from the bowel to another loop, organ (bladder, vagina) or skin – Crohn, diverticulitis, tumour.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Colon tumour

Irregular lacunar defect/stenosis with destroyed mucosa and heterogeneous mass on CT.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Lacunar image (filling defect)

LACUNA = filling (subtraction) defect inside the lumen – polyp, tumour, foreign body; opposite of the addition image (niche, diverticulum).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Corkscrew oesophagus

Diffuse oesophageal spasm: multiple non-propulsive tertiary contractions giving a corkscrew/rosary appearance.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Achalasia

Barium: dilated, elongated oesophagus with food/air–fluid level, absent gastric air bubble, smooth SHORT tapered "bird's beak" at the LES; no peristalsis.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Benign oesophageal stenosis

Axial, smooth, symmetric, LONG, progressive (tapered) narrowing, usually distal (peptic, caustic), upstream dilatation.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Benign gastric ulcer (Hampton line)

Niche projecting OUTSIDE the gastric contour, thin lucent Hampton line at its base, smooth radiating folds reaching the crater, ulcer collar/mound.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
HCC on hepatospecific contrast

Hepatocellular carcinoma lacks functioning hepatocytes → hypointense in the hepatobiliary phase (gadoxetic acid).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric tumour

Focal wall thickening/mass with irregular mucosa; CT staging – extension, nodes, metastases.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Oesophageal cancer

Irregular, eccentric, abrupt ("shouldered") stenosis or lacunar defect with mucosal destruction, rigid wall; CT/EUS/PET for staging.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Benign oesophageal tumour

Smooth, rounded submucosal filling defect with obtuse/right angles to the wall and intact mucosa (leiomyoma).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Paralytic vs mechanical ileus

Mechanical: dilated loops proximal to the obstacle, many air–fluid levels at different heights, collapsed distal bowel. Paralytic: diffuse gas in small bowel AND colon, fewer levels.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Sliding hiatal hernia

Gastro-oesophageal junction and cardia slide above the diaphragm (most common, reflux).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Mixed hiatal hernia

Both the gastro-oesophageal junction and part of the fundus herniate into the thorax.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric ulcer

Barium-filled niche (addition image) – benign outside the gastric contour with converging folds; malignant inside the contour with irregular folds.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric leiomyoma

Smooth submucosal mass with intact mucosa and right angles to the wall ± central ulceration (GIST/leiomyoma).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Duodenal tumour

Irregular filling defect/stenosis of the duodenum with mucosal destruction.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Chronic pancreatitis

Pancreatic CALCIFICATIONS, irregular moniliform dilatation of the Wirsung duct, atrophy, pseudocysts; focal form mimics carcinoma.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Coeliac disease

Small-bowel barium: dilated loops, flocculation/segmentation of barium, reduced jejunal folds ("ileal jejunisation", "moulage").

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric cancer

Barium: irregular lacunar defect, malignant ulcer within the contour with interrupted/clubbed folds, rigid wall; CT for staging.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Crohn disease

Terminal ileum: skip lesions, aphthous → deep longitudinal + transverse ulcers (cobblestone), "string sign" stenosis, fistulas; MR/CT enterography.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Colon cancer

Barium/CT colonography: irregular annular "apple-core" stenosis with overhanging edges, or polypoid lacunar defect; CT for staging.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver adenoma

Young woman on oral contraceptives; heterogeneous (fat, haemorrhage) arterial-enhancing lesion, hypointense on hepatobiliary phase; risk of bleeding/malignancy.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Ulcerative colitis

Continuous involvement from the rectum, fine granular mucosa, collar-button ulcers, pseudopolyps; chronic "lead-pipe" colon without haustra.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Ileocaecal tuberculosis

Thickened, contracted caecum and terminal ileum (Fleischner, "Stierlin" sign), incompetent ileocaecal valve.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Peutz-Jeghers polyposis

Multiple hamartomatous polyps (lacunar defects) of the small bowel; intussusception risk; mucocutaneous pigmentation.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Deep ulcers (barium)

Barium-filled niches projecting deep into the wall (collar-button ulcers in colitis).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver haemangioma

Most common benign liver tumour: well-defined hyperechoic lesion on US; CT/MRI peripheral nodular (globular) enhancement with centripetal fill-in; T2 "light bulb".

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver metastasis

Usually multiple nodules of varying size; hypoattenuating in the portal phase (most); hypervascular ones (NET, RCC, melanoma) enhance arterially. Often displace vessels.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Protrusion (bulge) – barium semiology

Contour bulge of a lumen caused by an extrinsic mass or a wall lesion.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Hepatocellular carcinoma

Cirrhotic liver; arterial-phase hyperenhancement + portal/delayed WASH-OUT + capsule (LI-RADS 5); portal vein tumour thrombus.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Crohn disease – cobblestone

Deep transverse and longitudinal ulcers separating oedematous mucosa = cobblestone pattern.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver metastases on SPIO MRI

SPIO (iron oxide) is taken up by Kupffer cells → normal liver darkens on T2; metastases (no Kupffer cells) remain bright.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
FNH on hepatobiliary contrast

Focal nodular hyperplasia is iso/HYPERintense on the hepatobiliary phase (contains hepatocytes + bile ductules) – distinguishes it from adenoma and metastases.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Ulcer (niche)

NICHE = addition image of barium in a mucosal defect; describe location (inside/outside contour), folds, Hampton line.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Rolling (para-oesophageal) hiatal hernia

Gastro-oesophageal junction stays below the diaphragm; the fundus rolls up beside the oesophagus (risk of volvulus).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver haemangioma

Most common benign liver tumour: well-defined hyperechoic lesion on US; CT/MRI peripheral nodular (globular) enhancement with centripetal fill-in; T2 "light bulb".

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Duodenal bulb ulcer

Barium niche in the bulb with radiating folds and deformed ("clover-leaf") bulb from scarring.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Colonic diverticulosis

Multiple round addition images (barium-filled outpouchings) mainly in the sigmoid; CT for diverticulitis.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver haemangioma

Most common benign liver tumour: well-defined hyperechoic lesion on US; CT/MRI peripheral nodular (globular) enhancement with centripetal fill-in; T2 "light bulb".

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Portal hypertension – collaterals

Cirrhosis with portosystemic collaterals (oesophageal/gastric varices, recanalised paraumbilical vein, splenorenal shunt), splenomegaly, ascites.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Oesophageal diverticulum

Addition image: Zenker (pharyngo-oesophageal, posterior), mid-oesophageal (traction), epiphrenic (pulsion).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver hydatid cyst

Well-delimited, encapsulated hypoechoic cystic lesion with septa (daughter cysts).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric tumour

Thickened gastric wall with a neoplastic mass.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Acute appendicitis (US)

Non-compressible appendix > 6 mm with thickened wall, hyperechoic inflamed peri-appendiceal fat and peri-appendiceal fluid.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Pneumoperitoneum

Crescent of free subdiaphragmatic air.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Small-bowel obstruction

Multiple air–fluid levels; mechanical ileus has more and larger fluid levels than paralytic ileus. Small bowel: central, valvulae conniventes crossing the whole lumen; colon: peripheral, haustra.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Achalasia (barium swallow)

Incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, absent normal peristalsis in the distal 2/3, dilated oesophagus ending in a short smooth "bird's beak".

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Achalasia (barium swallow)

Dilated oesophagus, air–fluid level, absent gastric air bubble, bird's beak.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Mid-oesophageal diverticulum (barium)

Addition image (outpouching) of the middle oesophagus (traction diverticulum).

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Benign oesophageal stricture (barium)

Axial, progressive, long, regular, distal narrowing with upstream dilatation.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Oesophageal cancer (barium)

Eccentric, irregular, abrupt ("shouldered") narrowing, usually < 6 cm, mild upstream dilatation, single.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Perforated gastric ulcer

Leak of gastric contents into the peritoneum: pneumoperitoneum and chemical peritonitis. Use water-soluble contrast, never barium, if perforation is suspected.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Colon cancer (barium enema)

Loss of haustration, irregular "apple-core" annular stenosis.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Liver cirrhosis

Ascites, splenomegaly, small right lobe with enlarged caudate/left lobe, irregular nodular contour. (Contrast: low-osmolar non-ionic iodinated.)

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Dilated intrahepatic bile ducts

Branching tubular structures parallel to portal veins ("double-barrel / too many tubes").

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Pancreatic tumour

Deformed pancreatic contour by a hypodense/hypoechoic mass.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Chronic pancreatitis

Dilated Wirsung duct, parenchymal calcifications, pseudocysts.

q: What is the diagnosis? Name the technique and the key sign.
a:
Gastric tumour (CT)

Large thick-walled gastric mass – stage it: extension, lymph nodes, metastases, operability.
